angle: Move from prohibition to structured use: rubrics, attribution, and audit trails.
sourceTitle: How to encourage smarter AI use in the classroom
linkedinPost:
Bans don’t build capability. Good guardrails do.

MIT Technology Review highlights how schools are shifting from blocking chatbots to teaching structured use—clear rubrics, attribution rules, and consequences. It’s a useful mirror for enterprises stuck between “no AI” and “use it everywhere.”

What works in production environments is very similar:
- Define allowed uses by task (drafting, summarizing, code scaffolding) with quality rubrics.
- Require attribution: “AI-assisted” tags and prompts preserved with the deliverable.
- Keep an audit trail: stored prompts/outputs linked to the ticket, not screenshots in DMs.
- Teach verification: sources, test cases, and a checklist for when to escalate to a human.

My take: enablement beats enforcement. The fastest teams I support didn’t wait for a perfect policy—they set a minimum viable one, measured errors and time saved, then iterated monthly.

If your policy can’t be explained on a single slide, people won’t use it—or they’ll work around it.

What’s on your one-slide AI use policy today? #AIAdoption #AIStrategy #EnterpriseAI
